title: AALP interface v2
description: Provider-agnostic external-API transport service, exposed to cross-protocol clients (primarily ACP) without depending on any AALP-private Python module, class, or on-disk state. This is the sole cross-protocol-supported surface of AALP; it deliberately excludes AALP's own administrative/credential functionality. Unlike interface v1, AALP is invoked as a short-lived subprocess per call rather than reached over a socket to a resident daemon -- there is no aalp.service, no listener, and no bearer-secret bootstrap. See 'transport_binding' and 'authentication' below, and interface/v2/README.md's Migration section for what this changes for a v1 client.

excluded_from_this_interface.credential.read: AALP-owned administrative functionality. Never exposed to cross-protocol clients through this interface, in any form.
excluded_from_this_interface.request.batch: Deferred. No genuine finite-batch need has been demonstrated by ACP yet; may become a new, additive, capability-gated operation in a later interface_version 2.x once one is.
excluded_from_this_interface.request.queue: Present in interface v1, REMOVED in v2 -- not deferred, not redefined. v1's coalescing (leader/joiner sharing one physical provider call) paid off only for concurrent identical requests observed inside one long-lived resident process holding a shared in-memory generation registry. A process-per-invocation CLI has no such registry and cannot observe 'concurrency' at all: by the time one invocation's process exists, runs, and exits, no other invocation is a live peer it could coalesce with. There is no daemonless analog to reintroduce this under; see README.md's Queue coalescing section.

authentication.mechanism: OS process/filesystem identity; no bearer secret, no socket, no bootstrap step
authentication.notes: Interface v1's bearer secret existed to authenticate an otherwise-anonymous socket client (any process reaching the loopback AF_UNIX socket). A CLI subprocess invocation has no equivalent anonymity to resolve: the OS starts it as, and it always runs as, the caller's own real uid/gid, and every filesystem access it makes (provider registry, credential store, admission lock files, maintenance flag, audit log) is mediated by the OS's own permission check on '.aalp/' -- the same 0600/0700 permission discipline aalp/credential.py and aalp/ingress.py already enforce on-disk. The trust boundary is therefore: whatever OS user (or root) owns and can read/write the target AALP root's '.aalp/' tree is implicitly authorized to invoke this interface against it; there is no separate per-call credential check inside AALP itself, because there is no longer a network-reachable listener for an unauthorized peer to reach in the first place. This is an authentication/bootstrap semantics change and is one of the reasons this is a new major interface version (see 'compatibility').

bootstrap.summary: None. There is no descriptor file, no secret file, and no discovery-before-first-call step -- a client that knows the AALP root (AALP_HOME env var, or an explicit --root argument, exactly as it would have needed to know before to interpret 'ingress.json') can invoke the CLI directly.
bootstrap.removed_files_notes: These three files were interface v1's entire bootstrap surface (adjustment metadata §4's one deliberate carve-out into '.aalp/'). None of them are written, read, or meaningful in interface v2; a v2 service need not even create '.aalp/state/' until its first admission or maintenance check touches it. A client must still never read or infer anything else from '.aalp/' state -- that restriction is unchanged, it just now has zero exceptions instead of one.

transport_binding.notes: request.forward's binding below is AALP's existing, already-implemented wire protocol and is normative: a conforming AALP service and a conforming fake service used for ACP client tests must both implement it exactly as described. provider.status and service.capabilities are discovery operations; the invocation/envelope pair given below is the concrete binding a fake service and the real AALP service must both implement, but a different transport encoding could replace the envelope format in a later interface_version without changing the operation names, fields, or outcome semantics documented here.

wire_protocol.kind: one short-lived child process per call, communicating over its own stdin/stdout -- not a socket, not HTTP, not a resident listener

invocation.argv_contents: Exactly two kinds of thing may appear in argv: the fixed literal tokens ('call', the operation name) and non-secret filesystem-path overrides ('--root', '--providers-dir', mirroring aalp/serve.py's existing flags). Nothing else is ever passed as a command-line argument.
invocation.argv_prohibition: NOTHING SENSITIVE MAY TRAVEL IN ARGV. This is a hard invariant, not an incidental choice: process argv is visible via 'ps'/'/proc/<pid>/cmdline' to every user on the host, unlike a byte stream piped directly between two processes' file descriptors. provider_id, method, path, headers (including any value forwarded upstream as an auth header), and body -- everything interface v1 sent inside its length-prefixed JSON frame -- go on stdin in interface v2 instead, for exactly this reason. A conforming client implementation must never format any of these into a command-line argument, an environment variable read from a shared process listing (AALP_HOME is a path, not a secret, and is the one exception), or any other channel readable by another user on the same host.
invocation.exit_semantics: Exactly one invocation performs exactly one operation and then exits; there is no keep-alive, no connection reuse, and no batching of multiple operations into one process lifetime.

request_envelope.transmitted_via: stdin, as a single UTF-8-encoded JSON object, EOF-terminated (the process reads until stdin closes, then parses; there is no length prefix -- a subprocess pipe has no framing ambiguity a length prefix would resolve, unlike the multiplexed socket connections interface v1's framing was written for)
request_envelope.client_obligation: NORMATIVE: a conforming client MUST close its end of the child's stdin immediately after writing the complete request envelope. The child process's read loop has no way to distinguish 'the client has more to write but is slow' from 'the client is never going to close this' -- both look identical from inside a blocking read-until-EOF loop -- so a client that writes the envelope and leaves stdin open hangs the child indefinitely with no way for the child itself to detect or recover from it. 'deadline_handling' below covers a client bounding its own wait for the child to exit, which limits the damage from a client failing this obligation, but does not substitute for it: a client that never closes stdin has produced a malfunctioning call regardless of what timeout it separately enforces on the read side.

fields.provider_id: string, required for request.forward, optional for provider.status (absent selects the list form), absent/ignored for service.capabilities and service.maintenance
fields.method: string, e.g. 'GET' or 'POST'; required for request.forward, absent for the other three operations
fields.path: string, the upstream path to request -- must be one of the target provider's accepted_paths; required for request.forward, absent for the other three operations
fields.headers: object of string to string; forwarded upstream verbatim on request.forward (minus AALP's own auth-header override, exactly as in v1), absent/ignored for the other three operations
fields.body: string, base64-encoded request body bytes (absent or empty string if there is no body); meaningful only for request.forward

response_envelope.transmitted_via: stdout, as a single UTF-8-encoded JSON object, written once and then the process exits; nothing is written to stdout before the complete envelope is ready to emit, and nothing is written to stdout afterward

fields.status: integer, an HTTP-style status code, meaning identical to interface v1's response_envelope.status
fields.headers: object of string to string; carries 'X-Aalp-Outcome' for request.forward responses exactly as in v1 (the header name is unchanged even though there is no HTTP header transport underneath -- it remains a JSON field name, matching v1's own already-informative-not-literal use of 'headers' for this purpose)
fields.body: string, base64-encoded response body bytes (empty string if there is no body)

wire_protocol.stderr: Diagnostic/human-readable text only (e.g. a malformed-invocation message). A conforming client must never parse stderr or key any behavior off its contents; stderr is not part of this contract's response shape.

exit_codes.0: The process ran the requested operation to completion and wrote a complete, well-formed response envelope to stdout. This is true even when that envelope's own 'status'/outcome represents an AALP-level failure (e.g. 'unavailable', 'upstream_error') -- exactly as, in v1, a non-success X-Aalp-Outcome was still delivered over a successfully-completed socket round trip. A client must inspect the response envelope's own fields to learn the outcome; exit code 0 says only that the envelope itself is trustworthy.
exit_codes.1: The invocation itself was malformed before any operation could run -- an unknown operation name, missing/invalid argv, or stdin that could not be parsed as the required JSON object. Nothing is written to stdout in this case; a diagnostic appears on stderr only.
exit_codes.2: An internal error occurred while producing a response for an otherwise well-formed invocation (the closest analog to interface v1's ingress-level 500). Nothing meaningful is written to stdout in this case either.
exit_codes.other: Reserved. A conforming client must treat any nonzero exit code as 'no trustworthy response envelope was produced' and must not attempt to distinguish exit codes other than 0 beyond that.

wire_protocol.deadline_handling: AALP's CLI process imposes no read/write deadline of its own on the exchange itself; all queue_timeout/compression_timeout/total_timeout budget enforcement is the client's responsibility, exactly as in v1 -- but now also including the client's own responsibility to bound how long it waits for the child process to exit at all (e.g. via its own process-level timeout/kill), since there is no longer a persistent server-side connection whose closure alone signals completion.

transport_binding.reserved_path_prefix_rule: Not applicable in interface v2. v1's '_aalp' reserved path-segment prefix existed to disambiguate discovery operations from request.forward's provider-passthrough paths inside one shared HTTP-style path namespace ('/{provider_id}/{upstream_path}' vs '/_aalp/v1/...'). v2's request envelope selects the operation explicitly (the CLI's <operation> argument), and provider_id/path are separate JSON fields rather than one combined path string, so there is no shared namespace left to disambiguate. A provider id is no longer restricted from beginning with '_' by this contract; nothing in v2 depends on that restriction.

scheduling_model.description: Requests targeting the same provider are each admitted into one of that provider's concurrency_limit admission slots before being forwarded; AALP never starts more than concurrency_limit simultaneous upstream requests for a given provider. Unlike interface v1, admission is NOT first-in-first-out: with N independent, short-lived CLI invocations polling for a free slot with no shared waiter registry between them, which waiter is admitted next depends on OS scheduling and polling timing, not on submission order. This is a per-provider guarantee, not a single global queue, exactly as in v1: different providers' requests may execute concurrently, and once a provider's concurrency_limit is greater than 1, that provider's own requests may too.
scheduling_model.ordering_guarantee: None. A caller must not assume that two requests submitted to the same provider in a given order will be admitted, start, or complete in that order, even under light contention. A waiting caller is also not guaranteed to make progress before its own deadline elapses under sustained contention from other waiters -- there is no fairness mechanism preventing one waiter from being repeatedly outrun by others' polling. This is a genuine behavioral loss versus v1's submitted-request-fifo guarantee, not a documentation change alone; a client that depended on FIFO ordering for correctness (as opposed to merely for throughput) cannot be ported to v2 without redesigning that dependency out.

flow_id.semantics: Unchanged from v1: a purely optional audit/grouping label. It confers no scheduling priority in v1 and confers none in v2 either -- this was already true before the ordering guarantee itself weakened, so no client behavior around this field needs to change.

scheduling_model.renewal_operation_notes: Interface v2 defines no renewal, lease-extension, or open-ended reservation operation, exactly as v1 did not. v1's README already stated that this removed per-flow reservation (the old X-Aalp-Flow-Token mechanism) may not be reintroduced without a new major interface version. Interface v2 IS that new major version, and this document makes the explicit decision required by that clause: the prohibition is CARRIED FORWARD, not lifted. No future v2.x addition may introduce a renewal/reservation operation of any kind without a new major version (v3). This is carried forward specifically because the daemonless model has, if anything, less to offer a reservation mechanism than v1 did: a FileLease (see README.md's Admission section) is held by one short-lived process for as long as that process runs, with no notion of 'the same logical holder reconnecting from a later call' to renew against -- reintroducing reservation semantics here would require designing an entirely new cross-process renewal primitive from scratch, not just un-deprecating v1's old one.
scheduling_model.concurrency_bound: Per active provider's declared concurrency_limit, discoverable via provider.status. The default 'ci' provider is concurrency_limit 1 (single-flight): AALP never starts a new upstream request for a provider beyond that provider's declared ceiling, and a caller's local timeout never by itself frees a slot that a not-yet-confirmed-closed upstream operation may still be occupying. Unchanged in meaning from v1; only the ordering of admission among waiters for that bound has changed (see 'ordering_guarantee').

outcomes.description: The closed set of outcomes request.forward may report, reusing aalp.errors.Outcome verbatim. No cross-protocol client should ever need to handle a value outside this set for request.forward, and no future v2.x addition may repurpose one of these values to mean something else. The set of values is unchanged from v1; one value's MEANING is narrowed because the mechanism it describes (FIFO admission) no longer exists -- see 'queue_timeout' below.

success.meaning: The request reached the provider and a response was read back completely. The upstream HTTP status code (e.g. a provider-side 4xx/5xx) is preserved as-is in the response and is NOT itself a non-success AALP outcome -- AALP classifies only transport-level results, never the provider's own application-level response.
success.response_status_code: passthrough (identical to the upstream response's status code)

unavailable.meaning: The target provider id is unknown or is currently marked inactive (providers/*.json 'active': false). No upstream network attempt was made.

queue_timeout.meaning: CHANGED FROM V1. The request could not be admitted into one of the target provider's concurrency_limit admission slots before its queue-timeout budget elapsed. No upstream network attempt was made. v1 described this as failing to be admitted into the provider's own FIFO lane; v2 has no FIFO lane to fail into -- admission in v2 is a bounded, best-effort race against other independent waiters for a free slot (see 'scheduling_model'), and this outcome fires when that race does not resolve to a free slot before the deadline. The outcome value name and response_status_code are unchanged; only the admission mechanism behind them is.

compression_timeout.meaning: An upstream network attempt was made and a connection-level timeout occurred while sending the request or reading the response (the upstream's own per-request timeout budget, distinct from the queue-wait budget).

total_timeout.meaning: The request's overall (queue + upstream) timeout budget elapsed. May occur either before an upstream attempt started (if admission alone exhausted the budget) or immediately after a slot was confirmed idle before any attempt was made.

invalid_response.meaning: An upstream network attempt was made and a connection was established, but the response could not be read/parsed as a well-formed HTTP response.

upstream_error.meaning: An upstream network attempt failed at the connection/transport level (DNS, TCP, TLS, or protocol-level failure) before any response was read.

maintenance.meaning: AALP's own maintenance-mode flag (see service.maintenance) was set at the moment this request was received. No upstream network attempt was made, and no provider- or admission-level check ran first -- maintenance mode pre-empts everything else in request.forward's pipeline.

service.capabilities.summary: Discover AALP's interface version and capability set.

capabilities.description: See top-level 'capabilities'. Absence of a capability string means a client must not assume that behavior is supported, even if it appears elsewhere in this document as a v2 concept. A v1 client that calls this against a v2 service will observe 'interface_version': 2 and 'request.queue' absent from the array -- this is how it should detect it is no longer talking to a v1-conformant service, if it checks (see README.md's Migration section).

outcomes.note: Not modeled with the request.forward Outcome enum. Exit code 0 with the body above is the only success case; a nonzero exit code (see transport_binding.exit_codes) is the only failure case -- there is no AALP-level outcome distinction here, same as v1.

provider.status.summary: Discover provider availability, concurrency state, and accepted request shape, so a client never needs to read providers/*.json directly.

binding.list_form: provider_id absent from the request envelope
binding.single_form: provider_id present in the request envelope

provider_id.description: When present (single form), scopes the response to one provider. When absent (list form), returns every provider AALP has loaded, active or not.

active.description: Whether request.forward will attempt this provider at all; false yields outcome 'unavailable'.

concurrency_limit.description: Maximum simultaneous in-flight upstream requests AALP will ever hold open for this provider.

in_flight.description: REMOVED FIELDS 'queued'/'idle_seconds' aside, semantically the same field v1 reported: currently held provider admission slots (upstream requests in progress, including quarantined/unconfirmed-closed ones). Computed differently than in v1: rather than reading one in-process counter, AALP probes each of this provider's concurrency_limit admission lock files with a non-blocking, non-exclusive (LOCK_SH|LOCK_NB) attempt, which succeeds-and-immediately-releases against a free slot and fails against a slot some process currently holds exclusively; in_flight is the count of slots that failed this probe. This is a best-effort point-in-time read, not an atomic snapshot across all concurrency_limit slots the way v1's single in-process lock made it -- a slot's held/free state can change between one slot's probe and the next, so a client observing this value while the provider is under contention should treat it as approximate, not as a linearizable count. This probe is read-only: it neither writes to nor otherwise mutates any admission lock file, on a free slot or a held one.

idle.description: True exactly when the probe described under 'in_flight' finds every slot free at the moment of the read. Subject to the same non-atomicity caveat as in_flight. Unlike 'idle_seconds' in v1, this is honestly answerable in the daemonless model: 'every slot probed free right now' needs nothing but the same read-only probe 'in_flight' already performs -- no history, no persisted timestamp, no cross-process record of anything that happened before this read.

accepted_paths.description: The exact upstream request paths request.forward will accept for this provider (the second path segment onward in v1's path-based routing; a plain string comparison against the request envelope's own 'path' field in v2 -- see transport_binding). Any other path yields outcome 'unavailable' for that provider.

removed_fields: queued -- REMOVED, not renamed and not reported as a permanent zero. See top-level 'excluded_from_this_interface' entry for request.queue is unrelated to this removal; this removal is about admission observability, not coalescing. v1's 'queued' meant 'requests currently waiting in this provider's FIFO lane' (contract.json v1 wording, verbatim). There is no FIFO lane in v2 to have a length: admission is N independent processes each independently polling N lock files with no shared waiter list anywhere for anyone to count. A permanent-zero 'queued' field was considered and rejected -- it would silently read as 'no backpressure right now' to any client using it that way, which is a stronger and false claim (there is no way to know whether zero, one, or a hundred other processes are currently polling for the same provider's slots). Removing the field outright is the only option that does not let a client draw a false conclusion from a value that looks like real data but isn't.

idle_seconds -- REMOVED, for the same reason as 'queued' and by the same owner decision, after a nullable design was drafted and rejected. v1 read this from one in-process 'last_activity' timestamp updated under a single process-wide lock; v2 has no such shared, always-live place to keep or update it. The specific mechanism that forecloses an honest number: a slot's holder can be killed (SIGKILL, OOM, host crash) at any point while holding the slot, and the OS lock exists specifically to survive that -- it is released instantly and unconditionally on process death, with no cleanup code run by anyone, because there is no cleanup code left to run once the process is dead. Any timestamp recording 'this slot became free at T' has to be written by somebody, and the only somebody in a position to write it -- the holder itself, on release -- is exactly the actor a crash prevents from running that write. A recorded-transition timestamp under that model does not degrade gracefully to 'approximate': it silently overstates idleness by precisely the interval between the crash and whenever a probe next reads it, in the unsafe direction (a caller treating a long idle_seconds as 'safe to treat this as dormant' would be told it has been quiet for longer than it actually has). There is no honest number obtainable here, at any precision, so v2 reports none -- not a plain number with a caveat, not a nullable field returning null only in the crash case. 'idle' is kept because it asks a strictly easier, currently-true-or-false question ('is every slot free right now') that a stateless read-only probe answers completely honestly with no history involved at all; 'idle_seconds' asks a question about the past that only a write nothing in this design can survive death to perform could answer. This is what makes the removal cheap rather than merely defensible: 'idle_seconds' has no consumer in either repo today. v1's gateway produces it (aalp/gateway.py) and aalp/lane.py computes it, but nothing reads it outside AALP's own status output, its own tests, and the fake-service fixture that exists only to satisfy this schema. ACP, the only cross-protocol client this interface is written for, never reads it. Removing a field that could sometimes be answered exactly is a real cost only if something is spending that exact answer; nothing is.
explicitly_excluded_fields: endpoint (AALP-internal upstream URL; not needed to use request.forward, and not exposed)

outcomes.note: Not modeled with the request.forward Outcome enum; plain 200 / 404 status codes inside the response envelope, exactly as in v1.

request.forward.summary: Submit one provider request and receive a documented outcome. The only operation that talks to a provider's upstream API.

binding.method_notes: any HTTP-style method string (forwarded verbatim to the provider), taken from the request envelope's 'method' field
binding.path_notes: the request envelope's 'path' field must exactly match one of the target provider's accepted_paths (see provider.status). Unlike v1, the provider is named by a separate 'provider_id' field, not by combining it into the same string as the upstream path -- see transport_binding.reserved_path_prefix.

provider_id.description: A top-level request-envelope field in v2 (was derived from the path's first segment in v1's wire form; already a separate logical field in v1's own operation-level schema).

path.description: Must be one of the target provider's accepted_paths.

X-Aalp-Flow-Id.description: Optional. See scheduling_model.flow_id. Never required, never a scheduling reservation.

X-Aalp-Queue-Key.description: REMOVED behavior in v2. This header is no longer inspected or special-cased at all -- v2 has no request.queue operation for its presence to select (see excluded_from_this_interface). A v1 client that sends it here gets it forwarded upstream verbatim like any other ordinary header, exactly as request.forward already treated any header it didn't specifically recognize. It is documented here only so a v1 client porting to v2 can see explicitly that this header now does nothing special, rather than discovering that silently.

headers.description: Forwarded upstream verbatim, except the provider's own declared auth header, which AALP overwrites with the credential it holds; a client must never attempt to set that header itself to authenticate with the provider.

body.description: Raw request body, forwarded upstream byte-for-byte unmodified on outcome 'success'. Transmitted base64-encoded inside the stdin JSON envelope, never as a command-line argument (see transport_binding.wire_protocol.invocation.argv_prohibition).

on_outcome_success.headers: passthrough (upstream response headers, verbatim) plus X-Aalp-Outcome: success

message.description: Non-normative diagnostic text; clients must key behavior off 'outcome', never off this string.

x_aalp_outcome_header.rationale: On outcome 'success', AALP passes the upstream status code through verbatim -- including a provider-side 4xx/5xx, which is a valid AALP-level success. Status code alone therefore cannot disambiguate an AALP-level failure (e.g. 502 upstream_error) from a provider that itself happened to return 502. X-Aalp-Outcome removes that ambiguity and must be present in the response envelope's 'headers' field on every request.forward response, success or not -- unchanged from v1, just a JSON field rather than a literal socket-framed header now.

service.maintenance.summary: Discover whether AALP is currently in maintenance mode, without needing to read its private `.aalp/state/maintenance` flag file directly.

outcomes.note: Not modeled with the request.forward Outcome enum. A reachable AALP service always exits 0 with the body above, even while in maintenance mode itself -- discovery is never blocked by maintenance mode.

compatibility.versioning: Interface major versions are protocol-local to AALP; they need not match ACP's or ADP's interface version numbers.

superseded_versions.1: SUPERSEDED, not coexisting. interface/v1/contract.json remains published in this repository as a historical record and is not deleted, but there is no longer a running service that implements it: the AF_UNIX-socket-plus-bearer-secret daemon (aalp.service) that interface v1's transport_binding and authentication sections describe is being removed entirely, on every platform, not just Windows. A client still targeting v1 has nothing left to connect to -- there is no dual-stack period where a caller can choose either interface against a live AALP. Every cross-protocol client must move to interface v2 as part of this migration; see interface/v2/README.md's Migration section for exactly what that requires.

stays_within_current_major_version_when_: existing outcomes retain their documented meaning
existing clients keep working without adopting any new capability
new fields are optional and/or gated behind a new capability string
service.capabilities exposes any newly added capability
requires_a_new_major_version_when_any_of: an operation or field is removed or renamed
an existing operation's or outcome's semantics change incompatibly
a previously valid request becomes invalid
